lecture.title: Gallbladder II: Cholecystitis, Mirizzi Syndrome, Bile Duct Stones, Cholangitis and Carcinoma
golden_tip: Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain = Charcot triad: ascending cholangitis until proven otherwise. Admit, rehydrate with IV fluids, start IV ceftriaxone and arrange urgent ERCP sphincterotomy for drainage.
Murphy's sign positive with fever and leukocytosis = acute cholecystitis. Chronic cholecystitis has NO fever and a NEGATIVE Murphy's sign - do not mix the two in the exam.

Golden period for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy = 2-5 days from onset of symptoms. Outside it: conservative Rx 2-3 days, then cholecystectomy after 6-8 weeks on a fat-free diet. Conversion to open is NOT failure.
Obstructive LFT pattern of bile duct stones: high bilirubin (mostly direct) and high alkaline phosphatase with normal or insignificant AST/ALT - this separates obstruction from hepatitis.

Jaundice + RUQ pain + fever with a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck = Mirizzi syndrome (external compression of CHD/CBD); MRCP and ERCP are both diagnostic, and it is also a cause of post-cholecystectomy biliary leak.

concepts.title: Acute Cholecystitis: Aetiology, Microbiology and Pathogenesis
concepts.summary_ar: التهاب المرارة الحاد هو التهاب حاد لجدار المرارة: حصوي في 85-95% من الحالات (حجر منحشر في جيب هارتمان أو ساد للقناة المرارية في 90%) وعديم الحصى في 5-15% (ركود ونقص تروية). الجراثيم بالترتيب: الإشريكية القولونية فالكلبسيلا فالعقدية البرازية فالبرويدات، ثم الكلوستريديا والتيفية وهي غير شائعة لكنها خطيرة. الأسباب الوعوية (سكري، فقر دم منجلي، ضغط مرتفع، أمراض كولاجين) تؤدي إلى خثار الشريان المراري فنقص التروية. وعواقب النوبة: هدواء، أو غرغرينا وموكوسيل وقيح، أو انثقاب، أو التهاب مزمن.

sections.heading: Definition and the Calculous-Acalculous Split (85-95% vs 5-15%)
sections.body_text: This is the second gallbladder lecture of the course (delivered by Dr Noori Henoon Jasim, FRCS, FACS, FICMS and PhD, United Kingdom, consultant gastrointestinal surgeon and associate professor), covering cholecystitis acute and chronic, postcholecystectomy syndrome, stones in bile ducts, ascending suppurative cholangitis and carcinoma of the gall bladder. **Acute cholecystitis is an acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall**. By frequency the disease splits into two forms: **calculous acute cholecystitis in 85-95% of cases**, in which one or more stones obstruct the cystic duct or lie impacted in Hartmann's pouch, and **acalculous acute cholecystitis in 5-15%**, in which no stone is found and the inflammation is driven by bile stasis, ischemia and bacterial proliferation in a distended, unemptied gallbladder. Acalculous disease classically appears in fasting, critically ill or injured patients (prolonged NPO status, sepsis, burns, major surgery, total parenteral nutrition) whose gallbladder never receives a cholecystokinin stimulus, so the bile thickens, sludges and becomes both chemically irritating and a culture medium. The pathogenesis shared by both forms follows one cascade: obstruction or dysfunction of the cystic duct, then mucus and bile accumulate, the gallbladder distends, intraluminal pressure rises, lymphatic and venous drainage of the wall is compromised, chemical inflammation of the mucosa begins, and bacteria invade, producing suppurative inflammation. If the cystic artery supply is additionally cut off, the wall becomes ischemic and then gangrenous. This cascade explains every clinical finding, investigation result and treatment step in the following concepts: the colicky pain and tender mass of a distended organ, the low-grade fever of a confined bacterial infection, and the need to drain or remove the gallbladder before gangrene or perforation occurs.
key_points: Acute cholecystitis = acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall.
Calculous form: 85-95% of cases (stone obstructing the cystic duct or impacted in Hartmann's pouch).
Acalculous form: 5-15% (stasis and ischemia in fasting or critically ill patients).
Cascade: cystic duct obstruction, distension, rising pressure, wall ischemia, chemical then bacterial inflammation.

check.prompt: In what percentage of cases is acute cholecystitis calculous (stone-related)?
check.explanation_ar: الشكل الحصوي يمثل 85-95% من حالات التهاب المرارة الحاد، بينما الشكل عديم الحصى (الركودي وناقص التروية) يمثل 5-15% فقط؛ لذلك نبحث عن الحصى أولًا في كل مريض.

sections.heading: Causative Microorganisms (M.O.) in Order
sections.body_text: The organisms responsible for acute cholecystitis, in the order given by the lecture, are: **1- Escherichia coli; 2- Klebsiella; 3- Streptococcus faecalis (the enterococcus); 4- Bacteroides; 5- Clostridia and typhoid, which are uncommon and serious**. The first three are enteric organisms that reach the gallbladder either by reflux up the biliary tree from the duodenum or through the portal venous blood; Bacteroides is the important anaerobe, particularly in severe or gangrenous disease. Clostridia are gas-forming anaerobes capable of producing emphysematous cholecystitis, classically in diabetic patients, and typhoid (Salmonella typhi) is carried chronically in the gallbladder, where the organism survives inside bile and seeds both chronic infection and stone formation; both are uncommon but serious, which is why the lecture singles them out. This microbiology is not academic trivia: it dictates the antibiotic plan of the conservative regimen, namely a third-generation cephalosporin such as **ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, or gentamicin**, with anaerobic cover added whenever Bacteroides or clostridia are suspected in severe or gangrenous disease. A blood culture growing E. coli or Klebsiella in a febrile patient with right upper quadrant pain should always raise the question of the biliary tree as the source.
key_points: Organisms in order: E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus faecalis, Bacteroides, then clostridia and typhoid.
Clostridia and typhoid are uncommon and serious (gas-forming emphysematous disease in diabetics; chronic typhoid carriage).
The organism list explains the antibiotic choice: ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or gentamicin.

sections.heading: Causes of Acute Cholecystitis and the Ischemic Endpoint
sections.body_text: The causes of acute cholecystitis are: **1- Stone in 90% of cases, impacted in Hartmann's pouch or obstructing the cystic duct**; **2- stasis**; **3- pancreatic juice reflux**; **4- a CBD stone**; **5- bacteremia**; and **6- the vascular effect of diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, hypertension and collagen disease, producing cystic artery thrombosis and ischemia** of the gallbladder wall. In the calculous 90% the stone physically blocks bile outflow at Hartmann's pouch (the pouch at the gallbladder neck) or within the cystic duct itself, so the gallbladder distends against a closed outlet. Stasis without a stone is the mechanism of acalculous disease described above. Pancreatic juice reflux occurs when pancreatic secretions track back up the common channel into the biliary tree and chemically inflame the gallbladder mucosa. A CBD stone causes obstruction downstream and engages the gallbladder by pressure and infection. Bacteremia seeds the gallbladder wall during systemic infection. The vascular group is the one students forget: the gallbladder is supplied by the cystic artery, effectively an end artery, so diabetic vasculopathy, sickle cell sludging and infarction, hypertensive arteriolar disease and collagen-vascular (vasculitic) injury can thrombose it, producing ischemic, often gangrenous cholecystitis with no stone at all - the classical route to gangrene in elderly diabetic patients.
key_points: Stone causes 90%: impacted in Hartmann's pouch or obstructing the cystic duct.
Non-stone causes: stasis, pancreatic juice reflux, CBD stone, bacteremia.
Vascular causes (DM, sickle cell, hypertension, collagen disease) lead to cystic artery thrombosis, ischemia and gangrene.

sections.heading: Sequelae of an Acute Attack
sections.body_text: Every attack of acute cholecystitis can end in one of four ways - the four sequelae of the attack. **1- Resolution**: the impacted stone disimpacts, drainage of the gallbladder resumes and the stone slips back into the body of the gallbladder, so the obstruction, distension and inflammation settle; this is the outcome in about 90% of conservatively treated attacks and is the reason a 2-3 day conservative trial is legitimate. **2- The impacted stone persists**, in which case continuing obstruction and inflammation progress to **gangrene** of the ischemic wall (especially in diabetics and the elderly), to **mucocele** (a chronically obstructed gallbladder distended with clear mucus once infection has been suppressed) or to **empyema** (the gallbladder filled with pus, the abscess of the gallbladder, giving high fever and a toxic patient). **3- Perforation** of the gangrenous wall, which may be walled off as a pericholecystic abscess or may leak freely to produce bile peritonitis, a surgical emergency. **4- Chronic cholecystitis**: repeated attacks heal by fibrosis, producing the thickened, fibrotic, shrunken gallbladder discussed in the next concept. Clinically this list is the justification for reviewing a conservatively managed patient every few hours: failure to improve within the expected 2-3 days signals that the stone remains impacted and that gangrene, empyema or perforation may be developing, at which point laparoscopic cholecystectomy or laparoscopic cholecystostomy must be performed.
key_points: Resolution (disimpaction, drainage, slipping back of the stone) occurs in about 90% of conservative trials.
Persistent impacted stone leads to gangrene, mucocele or empyema.
Perforation may produce a walled-off abscess or free bile peritonitis.
Repeated attacks lead to chronic cholecystitis.

concepts.title: Acute Cholecystitis: Clinical Features, Differential Diagnosis and Investigations
concepts.summary_ar: صورة التهاب المرارة الحاد السريرية اثنا عشر بندًا: بداية مفاجئة، العمر 30-70 سنة (وفي من تجاوز 60 سنة يشكل 25-35%)، البيض أكثر من السود، وجبة دسمة، ألم قولنجي، غثيان وقيء، حمّى خفيفة، علامة بواس، يرقان أحيانًا، علامة مورفي، إيلام وتصلب، وكتلة مؤلمة مجسوسة. والتشخيص التفريقي تسعة أمراض، والتأكيد بالأمواج فوق الصوتية (انتباج المرارة وسماكة الجدار وسائل محيط وحصى) مع تعداد كريات بيض مرتفع ووظائف كبد طبيعية تقريبًا.

sections.heading: Clinical Features - the Twelve Classic Findings
sections.body_text: The clinical features of acute cholecystitis are twelve, and examiners love them as a list. **1- Sudden onset** of symptoms, typically hours after the trigger. **2- Age 30-70 years**; and in patients older than 60 years acute cholecystitis accounts for **25-35%** of acute biliary presentations, so the elderly are over-represented among complicated cases. **3- White Caucasian patients are affected more than Black people**. **4- A heavy fatty meal** is the classical precipitant: fat in the duodenum releases cholecystokinin, which forces the gallbladder to contract against an obstructed cystic duct. **5- Pain that is colicky**, in the right hypochondrium. **6- Nausea and vomiting**. **7- Low-grade fever** - in the lecture's own case scenario the temperature is 37.8 C. **8- Boas's sign** - referred pain with hyperesthesia of the skin beneath the right scapula, due to irritation of the phrenic nerve supply of the diaphragmatic peritoneum overlying the inflamed gallbladder. **9- Jaundice occasionally**, which should always prompt a search for a coexisting CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome. **10- Murphy's sign** - the examiner hooks the fingers under the right costal margin and asks the patient to breathe in deeply; the descending, inflamed gallbladder touches the hand and inspiration abruptly stops with pain, and the sign is positive only on the right side. **11- Tenderness and rigidity** (guarding) over the right hypochondrium from localized peritoneal irritation. **12- A palpable tender mass** in a substantial minority of patients, representing the inflamed gallbladder wrapped in adherent omentum - an inflammatory mass that appears together with fever, distinguishing it from a malignant mass. Taken together: sudden right hypochondrial colicky pain after a fatty meal, with nausea, low-grade fever, positive Murphy's sign and tenderness in a middle-aged Caucasian woman is the textbook picture of acute calculous cholecystitis.
key_points: Sudden onset; age 30-70 years; above 60 years the disease makes up 25-35%; Caucasians more than Black patients.
Heavy fatty meal precipitates the attack (CCK contraction against an obstructed cystic duct).
Colicky right hypochondrial pain, nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever (37.8 C in the source case).
Boas's sign = referred hyperesthesia under the right scapula; Murphy's sign = inspiratory arrest under the right costal margin.
Occasional jaundice - look for a CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome.
Tenderness and rigidity; a palpable tender inflammatory mass.

sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis - Nine Mimics of Acute Cholecystitis
sections.body_text: Nine conditions must be differentiated from acute cholecystitis, each with a classical clue. **1- Appendicitis**: a high-lying or retrocecal appendix under the right lobe of the liver (or the appendix in a long pregnant uterus) mimics right upper quadrant pain; pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa with McBurney's point tenderness favors appendicitis. **2- Perforated peptic ulcer**: a perforated duodenal ulcer may leak bile-bearing fluid down the right paracolic gutter and produce right-sided signs; a history of epigastric pain and free subdiaphragmatic gas on an erect chest film favor perforation. **3- Acute right pyelonephritis**: fever with rigors, loin (costovertebral angle) tenderness and urinary symptoms with pyuria and bacteriuria favor the kidney. **4- Liver abscess**: swinging fever, tender hepatomegaly and an elevated right diaphragm with a right pleural reaction; imaging settles it. **5- Right lower lobar pneumonia**: basal pneumonia irritating the diaphragm refers pain to the right upper abdomen; respiratory signs and an infiltrate on chest imaging point to the lung. **6- Hepatitis**: viral hepatitis gives tender hepatomegaly with markedly raised transaminases (AST/ALT) rather than an obstructive pattern. **7- Pancreatitis**: epigastric pain boring to the back with raised amylase and lipase; remember that gallstones cause both diseases, so they can coexist in the same patient. **8- Herpes zoster**: dermatomal pain precedes the typical vesicular rash, and the tenderness is in the abdominal wall, not the viscera. **9- Myocardial infarction**: an inferior infarct can present as epigastric or right upper abdominal pain; an ECG is mandatory in atypical abdominal pain in elderly or diabetic patients. The exam skill is pairing each mimic with its discriminator: urinalysis for the kidney, erect chest film for the ulcer and the lung, ECG for the heart, amylase and lipase for the pancreas, LFT pattern for the liver, and ultrasound for the gallbladder.
key_points: DDx (9): appendicitis, perforated peptic ulcer, acute right pyelonephritis, liver abscess, right lower lobar pneumonia, hepatitis, pancreatitis, herpes zoster, myocardial infarction.
Each mimic has a discriminator: urinalysis, erect chest film, ECG, amylase and lipase, transaminase pattern, dermatomal rash, ultrasound.

sections.heading: Diagnosis: Ultrasonography, Liver Function Tests and WBC
sections.body_text: The diagnosis of acute cholecystitis rests on three investigations. **1- Ultrasonography is the first-line test** and shows four findings: a **distended gallbladder**, an **increase in wall thickness** from edema, a **pericholecystic fluid collection**, in addition to the **presence of a stone**, usually impacted at the neck or in the cystic duct. Ultrasound is inexpensive, bedside, radiation-free and interrogates the liver, bile ducts and pancreas in the same sitting, which is exactly why it is the correct next imaging test in the lecture's own case scenario. **2- Liver function tests (LFT)**: mostly no changes, or sometimes only little changes - significant jaundice or a rising bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase should redirect attention to a CBD stone, cholangitis or Mirizzi syndrome rather than uncomplicated cholecystitis. **3- WBC count: leukocytosis** - in the source case scenario the white cell count was 11000 with normal LFTs, a typical borderline-elevated laboratory picture. In practice amylase and lipase may be added to exclude concurrent gallstone pancreatitis, but the single best first investigation in suspected acute cholecystitis remains ultrasonography; MRCP is reserved for suspected duct stones, and ERCP is a therapeutic tool, not a screening test.
key_points: US features (4): distended gallbladder, increased wall thickness, pericholecystic fluid collection, stone.
LFT: mostly no or little changes; derangement suggests CBD stone, cholangitis or Mirizzi syndrome.
WBC: leukocytosis (source scenario 11000 with normal LFT).
US is the first-line imaging test; MRCP for duct stones; ERCP is therapeutic.

concepts.title: Acute Cholecystitis: Treatment and the Laparoscopic Approach
concepts.summary_ar: العلاج يبدأ تحفظيًا لمدة 2-3 أيام (صيام مع أنبوب أنفي معري، وسيفترياكسون أو سيفوتاكسيم أو جنتامايسين، ومسكن مع مضاد تشنج)، فيهدوء 90% من الحالات ثم يُستأصل بالتنظير بعد 6-8 أسابيع مع حمية خالية من الدهون، ومن لا يتحسن فالاستئصار أو الجلبي المراري بالتنظير. الفترة الذهبية للاستئصار المبكر هي 2-5 أيام من بدء الأعراض، والجراحة المفتوحة نادرة اليوم، ونسبة التحويل أعلى في الحاد لكن التحويل ليس فشلًا. وأثناء الجراحة يجب تحقيق المنظر الحرج للأمان قبل وضع القصاصات.

sections.heading: Conservative Treatment for 2-3 Days and the 90% Rule
sections.body_text: The treatment of acute cholecystitis begins with a structured conservative regimen lasting **2-3 days**, during which **90% of cases subside**. Its three components are: **1- an NG (nasogastric) tube and nil per mouth (NPO)** - resting the gut and the gallbladder, preventing further cholecystokinin-driven contraction against the obstructed duct and managing the ileus and vomiting; **2- antibiotics**, for example **ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or gentamicin**, chosen to cover the E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus faecalis and Bacteroides listed in the microbiology section; and **3- analgesia and an antispasmodic** to break the colicky pain of cystic duct obstruction. **If the patient improves**, the attack has resolved by disimpaction of the stone, and an **interval (delayed) laparoscopic cholecystectomy is performed after 6-8 weeks**; during this waiting period **the patient should be on a fat-free diet**, so that no fatty meal triggers a fresh attack of gallbladder contraction while the inflamed wall settles. **If the patient does not improve during or after these 2-3 days of conservative treatment**, the stone is still impacted and the gallbladder is heading toward gangrene or empyema, so the options become **laparoscopic cholecystectomy or laparoscopic cholecystostomy** - drainage of the gallbladder through a tube placed laparoscopically, chosen for the very unfit or high-risk patient in whom a full inflammatory dissection is judged too dangerous. Conservative treatment is therefore not passive waiting: it is a 2-3 day therapeutic trial with a predefined exit plan.
key_points: Conservative Rx for 2-3 days: NG tube and NPO; antibiotics (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or gentamicin); analgesia and antispasmodic.
90% of attacks subside on this regimen.
Improved: interval laparoscopic cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks with a fat-free diet in the interim.
Not improved during or after the 2-3 days: laparoscopic cholecystectomy or laparoscopic cholecystostomy.

sections.heading: Early Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy and the Golden Period (2-5 Days)
sections.body_text: **Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy** is performed when the patient presents **within the golden period of 2-5 days from the onset of symptoms**. Inside this window the gallbladder is edematous and vascular but not yet densely fibrosed, so the tissue planes around the cystic duct and artery can still be developed laparoscopically with an acceptable conversion rate; beyond day 5 the omentum and duodenum become plastered to the gallbladder with organized fibrosis, and early surgery becomes both harder and more dangerous, which is why such patients are sent down the conservative-then-interval pathway. **Nowadays the operation of choice is laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and open cholecystectomy is rarely performed** - reserved for situations where a laparoscopic service is not accessible or when conversion becomes necessary. Students must memorize the lecture's sentence about conversion: **the conversion rate in acute cholecystitis is higher than in elective surgery for other presentations, but conversion is still not a failure of laparoscopic cholecystectomy** - it is a sound safety decision made when the anatomy cannot be identified, when bleeding or injury threatens, or when the critical view of safety cannot be achieved. Converting early to protect the common bile duct is good surgery, not defeat.
key_points: Golden period = 2-5 days from onset of symptoms, for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Nowadays laparoscopic cholecystectomy is standard; open cholecystectomy is rare (inaccessible laparoscopy or conversion).
Conversion rate in acute cholecystitis is higher than elective.
Conversion is NOT failure - it is a safety decision.

sections.heading: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Calot's Triangle, Critical View of Safety and Ports
sections.body_text: The operative anatomy and safety technique of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, as illustrated in the lecture figures: The **anatomical schematic** shows the liver (brown) with the gallbladder/fossa area (green) and highlights two zones - the **hepatocystic triangle**, the larger triangular space, and **Calot's triangle**, the smaller, more specific triangle located within the hepatocystic triangle, **bounded by the cystic duct, the cystic artery and the common hepatic duct**. The **intraoperative laparoscopic view of the hilar region** identifies the following structures: the **base of liver segment 4** visible superiorly; the **cystic artery (CA)** branching towards the gallbladder; the **node of Lund (LN)**, the cystic lymph node; the **cystic duct (CD)** leading from the gallbladder; the **hepatic artery proper (HAP)**, the main arterial supply to the liver; and the **common bile duct (CBD)**, the main biliary drainage tube. The **critical view of safety** during dissection is achieved when the **hepatocystic triangle has been cleared of fat and fibrous tissue and only two structures are seen entering the gallbladder: the cystic duct and the cystic artery**, with the node of Lund also clearly visible in the dissected field. Only when this window is open - the gallbladder hanging from the cystic duct and artery alone, the base of segment 4 seen above and the common hepatic duct and CBD out of harm's way - may the clips be placed and the duct and artery divided; clipping any structure that has not been conclusively identified is how CBD injuries happen. The standard **four-port placement** seen in the clinical photograph of the abdomen: a **10 mm access port at or near the umbilicus** for the camera; a **10 mm right hand working port** in the upper right quadrant/epigastrium; a **5 mm left hand working port** in the left upper quadrant/epigastrium; and a **5 mm port for the fundus grasper** in the right flank/subcostal area, used to grasp the gallbladder fundus and retract it over the liver. The external surgical setup photograph shows the **trocars inserted** into the abdomen through these port sites, and the surgeon positioning photograph shows the **primary surgeon standing on the patient's left side**, holding the laparoscopic instruments in both hands while looking at the monitor.
key_points: Calot's triangle lies within the larger hepatocystic triangle and is bounded by the cystic duct, cystic artery and common hepatic duct.
Laparoscopic landmarks: segment 4 base, cystic artery, node of Lund, cystic duct, hepatic artery proper, CBD.
Critical view of safety = hepatocystic triangle cleared of fat and fibrous tissue; only CD and CA enter the gallbladder before clipping.
Ports: 10 mm umbilical camera port, 10 mm right hand working port, 5 mm left hand working port, 5 mm fundus grasper port; surgeon stands on the patient's left.

check.prompt: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, when has the surgeon achieved the critical view of safety?
options: When the gallbladder fundus is fully mobilized off the liver bed
When the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue and only the cystic duct and cystic artery are seen entering the gallbladder

sections.heading: Choosing the Operation - a Practical Decision Pathway
sections.body_text: Putting the treatment options into one decision pathway for exams and ward rounds: **A fit patient seen within the golden period (2-5 days from onset)** goes for **early laparoscopic cholecystectomy** after a short period of resuscitation, analgesia and antibiotics - the modern standard. **A patient seen after the golden period** is started on the conservative regimen (NG tube, NPO, ceftriaxone/cefotaxime/gentamicin, analgesia and antispasmodic) for **2-3 days**; if the expected resolution follows, the gallbladder is removed electively **6-8 weeks later**, with the patient maintained on a **fat-free diet** in the interval. **A patient who fails to improve during or after the 2-3 conservative days** needs the gallbladder dealt with during the same admission: **laparoscopic cholecystectomy**, or **laparoscopic cholecystostomy** if the patient is too unfit for a full dissection or the anatomy is too hostile - the drain can later be removed once the tract matures and the acute illness has settled. In every branch the operation of choice is laparoscopic; **open cholecystectomy is the fallback** for non-accessible laparoscopy or for conversion, and a conversion, as stressed before, is a safety decision rather than a failure.
key_points: Within the golden period: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Outside it: conservative trial for 2-3 days.
Conservative success: interval laparoscopic cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks on a fat-free diet.
Conservative failure: same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy or laparoscopic cholecystostomy.
Laparoscopic is the default; open is for non-accessible laparoscopy or conversion.

concepts.title: Chronic Cholecystitis and Saint Triad
concepts.summary_ar: التهاب المرارة المزمن: جدار ليفي سميك في مرارة متقلصة تحوي حصى؛ نوبات ألم يمينية تحت الضلع متغيرة الشدة والفاصل تدوم كل منها 3-12 ساعة، مع عسر هضم انتفاخي (امتلاء وتجشؤ وحرقة وتطبل) وغثيان، دون حمّى ودون علامة مورفي موجبة. الأمواج فوق الصوتية تُظهر تقلص المرارة رغم صيام 8 ساعات مع سماكة الجدار والحصى، والتحاليل طبيعية، والعلاج استئصار المرارة بالتنظير. ومثلث سانت (حصى المرارة مع انتباغات القولون مع فتق حجابي) يذكّر بتحديد المسبب الحقيقي لعسر الهضم قبل الجراحة.

sections.heading: Pathology and Symptom Profile of Chronic Cholecystitis
sections.body_text: Chronic cholecystitis is the long-run counterpart of the acute disease: repeated attacks of inflammation heal by fibrosis, leaving **a thickened, fibrotic wall with overall shrinkage (contraction) of the gallbladder, containing stone or stones**. Its symptom profile differs sharply from the acute form. **1- Pain: episodes of right hypochondrial pain of varying severity and interval, each lasting 3-12 hours**, characteristically after meals; the attacks are milder and less frequent than an acute attack, and by the time the patient reaches the surgeon the findings may have melted away. **2- Flatulent dyspepsia**: fullness after meals, belching, heartburn and abdominal distension - the fat-intolerance complex. **3- Nausea and vomiting**. **4- No fever** - chronic cholecystitis is not active infective inflammation, so the patient is afebrile. **5- Negative Murphy's sign** - the gallbladder wall is not acutely inflamed enough to stop inspiration. This fever-free, Murphy-negative, recurring-episode picture is the exam discriminator from acute cholecystitis, in which fever and a positive Murphy's sign are the rule. The classical trap is to dismiss these patients as simple dyspepsia; the correct habit is to send every patient with recurrent biliary-type dyspepsia for an ultrasound, because the stones are still present, still symptomatic and still capable of producing acute cholecystitis, pancreatitis or a CBD stone.
key_points: Chronic cholecystitis = thickened fibrotic wall of a shrunken gallbladder with stone(s).
Recurrent right hypochondrial pain episodes of varying severity and interval, each 3-12 hours, after meals.
Flatulent dyspepsia: fullness, belching, heartburn, distension; plus nausea and vomiting.
NO fever and NEGATIVE Murphy's sign - the contrast with acute cholecystitis.

check.prompt: Which pair of findings most clearly distinguishes chronic from acute cholecystitis?
options: Absence of fever with a negative Murphy's sign
Right hypochondrial pain after fatty meals
Female sex and age above 40 years
check.explanation_ar: الفرق المفصلي أن الالتهاب المزمن لا يترافق مع حمّى ولا مع علامة مورفي موجبة لأن الالتهاب ليس حادًا فعّالًا، بينما الألم والحصى والغثيان مشتركة بين الشكلين.

sections.heading: Investigations and Treatment of Chronic Cholecystitis
sections.body_text: The investigations of chronic cholecystitis are three. **1- Ultrasonography** shows **shrinkage of the gallbladder in spite of fasting for 8 hours**, together with a **thick gallbladder wall** and the **presence of stones**. The fasting detail is the sonographic key: a normal gallbladder, given 8 hours without food, should be full and distended with stored bile; a gallbladder that remains contracted in spite of an 8-hour fast has a fibrotic, non-compliant wall that cannot accommodate bile - that is chronic cholecystitis in a single image. **2- A normal WBC** count, because there is no active infection. **3- Normal liver function tests (LFT)**, because the disease is confined to the gallbladder; deranged LFTs would again point to a CBD stone or cholangitis rather than to chronic cholecystitis. The treatment of chronic cholecystitis is **laparoscopic cholecystectomy** - the stones are symptomatic and the attacks recur, and an elective operation on a chronically inflamed but quiescent gallbladder is far easier and safer than operating in the heat of an acute attack. There is no role for expectant management in a fit symptomatic patient, because delaying surgery only invites one of the acute complications - acute cholecystitis, empyema, pancreatitis or a migrated duct stone.
key_points: US: shrunken gallbladder in spite of 8 hours of fasting + thick wall + stones.
Normal WBC and normal LFT.
Treatment: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

sections.heading: Saint Triad - Gallstones, Diverticulosis and Hiatus Hernia
sections.body_text: **Saint triad** is the association of three causes of dyspepsia in the same patient: **1- gallstone or gallstones; 2- diverticulosis (of the colon); 3- hiatus hernia**. The lecture's warning follows directly: **it is important to find which one is the cause of the dyspepsia**, because all three produce nearly identical upper abdominal symptoms - fullness, belching, heartburn and post-prandial discomfort. If the wrong culprit is blamed, the patient undergoes cholecystectomy (or hernia repair) and returns with the same dyspepsia - one of the recognized roads into post-cholecystectomy syndrome, in which 15% of cholecystectomies fail to relieve symptoms, with Saint's triad listed first among its causes. The workup is therefore deliberate: an ultrasound documents the stones, endoscopy or a barium swallow evaluates the hiatus hernia, and a colon study assesses the diverticulosis, after which the symptom timeline and the food triggers are matched to the offending organ before any operation is offered. Saint triad is a favorite exam association (named after the Irish surgeon C.F.M. Saint) and it links this concept to the complications concept: it is simultaneously a differential diagnosis of gallbladder-type dyspepsia and the leading listed cause of persistent symptoms after the gallbladder has been removed.
key_points: Saint triad = gallstones + diverticulosis + hiatus hernia.
All three cause dyspepsia; identify the true culprit before operating.
Unrecognized Saint triad is the first listed cause of post-cholecystectomy syndrome.

check.prompt: Which triplet makes up Saint triad?
options: Gallstones, diabetes and sickle cell anaemia
Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
Gallbladder cancer, liver cyst and colonic polyp

concepts.title: Mirizzi Syndrome, Post-Cholecystectomy Complications and Indications for Cholecystectomy
concepts.summary_ar: متلازمة ميريزي: حجر منحشر في القناة المرارية أو عنق المرارة يضغط القناة الكبدية الجامعة أو الجامعة للصفراء فيسبب انسدادًا ويرقانًا (أنواع من الأول إلى الخامس)، وأعراضها يرقان وألم وحمّى، وتشخيصها بالتحاليل والأمواج والـMRCP والـERCP وكلاهما تشخيصي، وعلاجها استئصار المرارة مع أو بدون استكشاف القناة الجامعة وإصلاحها. مضاعفات استئصال المرارة: نزف ويرقان وإصابة الأعضاء المجاورة وتسرب صفراوي (قصاصات زاحلة أو قناة إضافية أو إصابة القناة الجامعة ونقص ترويتها أو متلازمة ميريزي) ومتلازمة ما بعد الاستئصار التي لا تخفف أعراض 15% بسبب سبعة أسباب. ودواعي الاستئصار: حصى عرضية، أو صامتة مع سكري أو فقر دم منجلي، أو وقائي جدلي في جراحة البدانة المفرطة، أو سرطان المرارة مع استئصار إسفيني لفراش الكبد.

sections.heading: Mirizzi Syndrome - Definition, Types and Clinical Features
sections.body_text: **Mirizzi syndrome (also spelled Mirrizi)** is a rare condition in which **a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or in the neck of the gallbladder causes compression of the common hepatic duct (CHD) or the common bile duct (CBD), resulting in CBD obstruction and jaundice**. The obstruction is extrinsic - the stone itself never leaves the cystic duct, but together with the surrounding inflammation it presses on the adjacent duct, which runs close and parallel to the cystic duct within the hepatocystic triangle. The lecture classifies the syndrome into **types I, II, III, IV and V, as illustrated in the photo**; because that figure carries no extracted text, the standard Csendes classification is given here for completeness: **Type I** - simple external compression of the CHD or CBD by the impacted stone with pericholecystic inflammation, and no fistula (the commonest type); **Type II** - a cholecystocholedochal fistula has formed as the stone erodes through, involving less than one-third of the bile duct circumference; **Type III** - the fistula involves up to two-thirds of the duct wall; **Type IV** - complete circumferential destruction of the bile duct wall; **Type V** - any of the above types combined with a cholecystoenteric fistula into the duodenum or colon (subdivided in some series into V-a without and V-b with gallstone ileus). The clinical features (C/F) of Mirizzi syndrome are **jaundice, pain and fever** - the same triad that mimics a CBD stone with cholangitis, which is why imaging of the ducts is mandatory before any operation. Mirizzi matters twice in this lecture: once as a cause of obstructive jaundice in its own right, and once as a mechanical cause of biliary injury and leak during cholecystectomy, because the inflamed, distorted anatomy drags the CBD toward the neck of the gallbladder and invites the surgeon to misidentify and injure it.
key_points: Mirizzi = a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compressing the CHD or CBD, causing obstruction and jaundice.

Types I-V: I external compression; II fistula under one-third of the circumference; III up to two-thirds; IV complete destruction; V any type with cholecystoenteric fistula (standard Csendes classification, photo not text-extracted).
C/F: jaundice, pain and fever.
A recognized hazard that makes CBD injury more likely during cholecystectomy.

check.prompt: What is the essential mechanism of Mirizzi syndrome?
options: A stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck externally compressing the CHD or CBD
A primary stone formed inside the common bile duct
A stricture of the sphincter of Oddi
A cholecystoenteric fistula without any impacted stone
check.explanation_ar: جوهر متلازمة ميريزي هو حجر منحشر في القناة المرارية أو عنق المرارة يضغط من الخارج على القناة الكبدية الجامعة أو الجامعة للصفراء فيسبب انسدادًا ويرقانًا دون أن يكون الحجر داخل القناة نفسها.

sections.heading: Mirizzi Syndrome - Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.body_text: The investigations for Mirizzi syndrome: **1- CBC (increased WBC)** - the leukocytosis of the accompanying inflammation - and **LFT changes with increased bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase**, an obstructive (cholestatic) pattern identical to that of a CBD stone. **2- Ultrasonography**, which may show the impacted stone at the neck or cystic duct with dilatation of the biliary tree above the level of compression. **3- MRCP and ERCP - both are diagnostic**: MRCP non-invasively demonstrates the extrinsic compression, the dilated ducts and any fistulous communication; ERCP is simultaneously diagnostic and therapeutic - it outlines the anatomy, can decompress and stent the duct, and thereby guides the surgical plan. The treatment is **cholecystectomy and/or CBD exploration**: **removal of the stone/s from the CBD followed by CBD repair**, and the lecture gives **choledochoduodenostomy** as the example of such a repair - a biliary-enteric anastomosis draining the duct into the duodenum when the duct wall is damaged or must be bypassed. In the higher types (III and IV), the repair may require more complex biliary-enteric reconstruction, and the full extent of the disease is often only established intra-operatively, which is exactly why intraoperative cholangiography is recommended when Mirizzi is suspected: **the anatomy must be defined before any duct is cut**.
key_points: Ix: CBC (raised WBC); LFT with raised bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; ultrasound; MRCP and ERCP - both diagnostic.
Rx: cholecystectomy and/or CBD exploration with removal of the stones followed by repair, e.g. choledochoduodenostomy.
Define the anatomy (cholangiography) before dividing any duct.

sections.heading: Post-Cholecystectomy Complications and the Four Causes of Biliary Leak
sections.body_text: The post-cholecystectomy complications are five. **1- Bleeding** - from the cystic artery, the liver bed or a port site, presenting as intra-abdominal hematoma or shock in the early postoperative hours. **2- Jaundice** - postoperative jaundice demands a structured search: a retained CBD stone, a clipped or injured CBD, or a leaking duct with bile accumulating under pressure. **3- Adjacent organs injury** - the duodenum, colon, small bowel or liver can be injured during port insertion or dissection. **4- Biliary leak progressing to a fistula**, whose four causes must be memorized in the lecture's order: **(a) slipped clips, or rarely a slipped ligature**, when occlusion of the cystic duct stump fails; **(b) an accessory duct** - a small aberrant duct of the liver bed, never identified and therefore never clipped; **(c) CBD injury or ischemia** - a divided, burned or devascularized duct; and **(d) Mirizzi syndrome**, whose inflamed anatomy predisposes to misidentification and injury of the CBD at operation. A biliary leak presents with bile in the drain, bile-stained ascites, peritonitis, fever and progressive jaundice, and is confirmed and often treated by ERCP (stenting across the leak) with percutaneous drainage of collections. **5- Post-cholecystectomy syndrome**, the persistence or recurrence of symptoms after the gallbladder has been removed, detailed in the next section.
key_points: Complications: bleeding, jaundice, adjacent organs injury, biliary leak leading to fistula, post-cholecystectomy syndrome.
Biliary leak causes (4): slipped clips or rarely ligature; accessory duct; CBD injury or ischemia; Mirizzi syndrome.

sections.heading: Postcholecystectomy (Post-Cholecystectomy) Syndrome - 15% and Its Seven Causes
sections.body_text: **Postcholecystectomy syndrome** (the slide heading reads post cholecystostomy syndrome, but it refers to the syndrome after cholecystectomy) means that **15% of cholecystectomies fail to relieve the patient's symptoms**. The seven causes must be memorized: **1- Saint's triad** - the diverticulosis or the hiatus hernia, not the stones, was the true cause of the dyspepsia; **2- pancreatitis**, including gallstone pancreatitis and pancreatic disease; **3- D.U. - duodenal ulcer** - masquerading as biliary pain; **4- a CBD stone**, retained or newly formed; **5- a long cystic duct stump** - a residual stump long enough to form a small symptomatic reservoir (stump syndrome); **6- a CBD stricture**, ischemic or post-injury; and **7- fibrosis of the sphincter of Oddi**, impairing bile drainage at the ampulla. The clinical approach to such a patient is to re-take the history (was the pain ever truly biliary?), repeat LFTs and ultrasound, and progress to MRCP or ERCP to interrogate the ducts. Note how this list unites the whole lecture: Saint triad from the chronic cholecystitis concept, Mirizzi and CBD injury from the complications concept, and the duct-stone pathology of the next concept all reappear here as reasons a cholecystectomy can leave the patient unimproved.
key_points: 15% of cholecystectomies fail to relieve symptoms.
Causes (7): Saint triad; pancreatitis; duodenal ulcer; CBD stone; long cystic duct stump; CBD stricture; fibrosis of the sphincter of Oddi.

check.explanation_ar: من أسباب متلازمة ما بعد استئصال المرارة: بقايا قناة مرارية طويلة، وحصى أو تضيق في القناة الجامعة، وتليف عاصرة أودي، وتقرح الاثني عشر، والتهاب البنكرياس، وثلاثية سانت؛ أما القناة القصيرة فهي هدف الجراحة السليم.

sections.heading: Indications for Cholecystectomy
sections.body_text: The indications of cholecystectomy in general are four. **1- Symptomatic gallstones**: pain, complications or sequelae attributable to stones justify removing the gallbladder - this covers acute cholecystitis, chronic cholecystitis and recurrent biliary colic. **2- Asymptomatic gallstones with diabetes mellitus and sickle cell anaemia**: in these groups the complications of an acute attack are dangerous (diabetics develop gangrenous and emphysematous cholecystitis with silent atypical presentations, and sickle cell patients suffer repeated crises that both mimic and worsen biliary inflammation), so the stones are removed before they become dangerous. **3- Prophylactic cholecystectomy - controversial - as in morbid obesity surgery**: rapid weight loss after bariatric operations precipitates gallstone formation in a substantial fraction of patients, so some surgeons remove the gallbladder concomitantly or plan for it later; because the risk-benefit balance is debated, the lecture explicitly labels this indication controversial. **4- Carcinoma of the gallbladder**, where the operation is necessarily bigger than a simple cholecystectomy: it is **accompanied by a wedge resection of the liver bed** (with excision of the gallbladder liver bed and hilar lymphadenectomy, as detailed in the carcinoma concept). For every other asymptomatic patient with an incidental stone and no risk factors, observation remains the default, because the lifetime risk of developing symptoms is modest.
key_points: 1- Symptomatic gallstones.
2- Asymptomatic gallstones with diabetes mellitus and sickle cell anaemia.
3- Prophylactic cholecystectomy (controversial), e.g. in morbid obesity surgery.
4- Gallbladder carcinoma - with wedge resection of the liver bed and hilar lymphadenectomy.

key_terms.definition_ar: حجر منحشر في القناة المرارية أو عنق المرارة يضغط القناة الكبدية الجامعة أو الجامعة للصفراء مسببًا يرقانًا انسداديًا؛ النوع الأول ضغط خارجي، والأنواع الثاني إلى الرابع ناسور متزايد الاتساع، والخامس مع ناسور مراري معوي.
القناة الكبدية الجامعة التي تجمع قنوات الكبد اليمنى واليسرى قبل اتصالها بالقناة المرارية لتكوين الجامعة للصفراء.
قناة صفراوية إضافية صغيرة تصب من فراش الكبد مباشرة في المرارة أو القناة المرارية؛ إن لم تُقصّ تتسبب بتسرب صفراوي بعد الجراحة.
قصاصات زاحلة عن جذمور القناة المرارية بعد الجراحة، وهي أشيع أسباب التسرب الصفراوي والناسور الصفراوي.
استمرار الأعراض بعد استئصال المرارة في نحو 15% من المرضى؛ أسبابها سبعة أبرزها ثلاثية سانت وحصى القناة الجامعة وبقايا قناة مرارية طويلة.
مفاغرة بين القناة الجامعة للصفراء والاثني عشر لإصلاح القناة أو تجاوز تضيقها، كما في متلازمة ميريزي وبعد استكشاف القناة.
استئصال العقد اللمفية البابية (نقرة الكبد)، وهو جزء من جراحة سرطان المرارة.

concepts.title: Stones in the Bile Ducts (Choledocholithiasis): Obstructive Jaundice, Charcot Triad and Clearance of the Duct
concepts.summary_ar: حصى القنوات الصفراوية (أولية أو ثانوية لحصى المرارة) تؤدي أولًا إلى يرقان انسدادي ثم إلى التهاب القناة الصفراوية. الأعراض ثالوث شاركو: يرقان متقطع وألم قولنجي وحمّى مع رجفة. مضاعفاتها: التهاب القناة والتهاب البنكرياس والتشمع الصفراوي. التحاليل: ارتفاع البيليروبين والمباشر والفوسفاتاز القلوي مع AST وALT طبيعيين تقريبًا، والأمواج تُظهر اتساع القناة الجامعة، والـMRCP يؤكد الحجر. العلاج: تنظير القنوات مع قطع العاصرة، وعند الفشل فتح القناة الجامعة فوق الاثني عشري مع أنبوب T أو مفاغرة قناة-اثني عشر، أو قطع العاصرة عبر الاثني عشر مع استخراج الحجر.

sections.heading: Primary and Secondary Duct Stones and Their Consequences
sections.body_text: **Stones in the bile ducts lead to obstructive jaundice firstly** - that is the opening sentence of the lecture and the key to the whole topic. Duct stones are **either primary or secondary to gallstones**: **primary stones** form within the bile ducts themselves, typically brown pigment stones growing in a duct that is dilated, strictured or stagnant, often with bacterial beta-glucuronidase activity deconjugating bilirubin; **secondary stones**, the commoner variety, are stones that formed in the gallbladder and migrated through the cystic duct into the common bile duct - they are the reason every jaundiced gallstone patient must have the duct imaged. The two consequences are **obstructive jaundice** (the stone blocks bile outflow, conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into the blood, and the patient turns yellow with dark urine and pale stools) **and cholangitis** (infected, stagnant bile behind the obstruction - the emergency detailed in the next concept). The obstruction of a duct stone is characteristically **intermittent**, because the stone can disimpact and reimpact, ball-valving at the ampulla: this explains the classical fluctuating jaundice far better than a fixed malignant stricture ever would, and intermittent jaundice in a gallstone patient should always suggest a duct stone.
key_points: Duct stones lead to obstructive jaundice firstly.
Primary = formed in the duct (pigment, stasis); secondary = migrated from the gallbladder (commoner).
Consequences: obstructive jaundice and cholangitis.
The obstruction is characteristically intermittent (ball-valve at the ampulla).

sections.heading: Symptoms - Charcot Triad - and Complications
sections.body_text: The symptoms of bile duct stones are three, and together they make up the classical **Charcot triad**: **1- jaundice, mostly intermittent**; **2- colicky pain**, as the duct distends and strains against the obstructing stone; and **3- fever and rigors**, bacteria proliferating in the stagnant bile entering the bloodstream - a rigor is the classical shaking chill of bacteremia. **Charcot triad means the duct stone has already complicated into cholangitis until proven otherwise**, and its completeness is a marker of severity. The three complications of duct stones are: **1- cholangitis**, which may progress to suppurative ascending cholangitis with septicemia; **2- pancreatitis**, when a small stone migrates further down and impacts at the ampulla of Vater, obstructing the pancreatic duct - gallstone pancreatitis; and **3- biliary cirrhosis**, the end result of long-standing untreated obstruction: retained bile inflames and fibroses the intrahepatic ducts and the liver parenchyma, with portal hypertension following after months to years. This complication trio explains why a duct stone is never simply observed: it must be extracted, by ERCP first and by surgery if ERCP fails.
key_points: Charcot triad: intermittent jaundice + colicky pain + fever and rigors.
Complications: cholangitis, pancreatitis, biliary cirrhosis.

check.prompt: Which triad is classically produced by a stone in the common bile duct with infected stagnant bile?
options: Charcot triad: jaundice, colicky pain, fever and rigors
Saint triad: gallstones, diverticulosis, hiatus hernia
Boas triad: scapular pain, fever, mass
check.explanation_ar: ثالوث شاركو هو يرقان متقطع غالبًا مع ألم قولنجي مع حمّى ورجفة؛ ووجوده يعني أن حصى القناة الجامعة قد تطورت إلى التهاب القناة الصفراوية ويستدعي تدخلًا عاجلًا.

sections.heading: Diagnosis - the Obstructive LFT Pattern, Ultrasound and MRCP
sections.body_text: The diagnosis of bile duct stones rests on three steps, and the LFT pattern is the exam favorite. **1- LFT: an increase in bilirubin, an increase in direct (conjugated) bilirubin and an increase in alkaline phosphatase, with normal or not significant changes in AST or ALT**. This is the pure obstructive (cholestatic) signature: the ductal enzyme alkaline phosphatase rises from pressure on the biliary epithelium, conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into the blood because outflow is blocked, while the hepatocyte transaminases AST and ALT remain essentially normal because the liver cells themselves are intact - contrast this with viral hepatitis, where AST and ALT soar while alkaline phosphatase stays near normal. **2- Ultrasound: showing a dilated CBD** - the duct dilates upstream of the obstruction (a normal CBD is slim, up to about 6 mm in caliber, and dilates progressively with obstruction and mildly with age); ultrasound also documents the dilated intrahepatic ducts and the gallbladder stones of origin, although the distal stone itself is often hidden behind duodenal gas. **3- MRCP to confirm the presence of a stone in the CBD**: it is non-invasive, requires neither contrast nor endoscopy, and is the confirmatory test of choice before any therapeutic ERCP is attempted.
key_points: LFT pattern: raised bilirubin (mostly direct) and raised alkaline phosphatase, with normal or insignificant AST/ALT changes.
US: dilated CBD (and dilated intrahepatic ducts).
MRCP: confirms the stone in the CBD before therapy.

sections.heading: Treatment - ERCP and Sphincterotomy First; Choledochotomy If Failed
sections.body_text: The treatment ladder of bile duct stones has two rungs. **1- ERCP and sphincterotomy** is the first-line treatment: at endoscopy the papilla is identified, the sphincter of Oddi is divided (sphincterotomy), and the stone is extracted with a basket or balloon, or crushed and removed; in the same sitting a stent or nasobiliary drain can be placed to decompress an infected system. **2- If ERCP fails** (a stone too large or impacted, intrahepatic stones, anatomical difficulty, or the service unavailable), **choledochotomy - open or laparoscopic CBD exploration - is performed**, and the lecture divides it into two approaches: **A- supraduodenal choledochotomy**: the duct is opened above the duodenum and the stone or stones removed (with irrigation, scoops or a balloon), after which either **a T-tube** is left draining the duct - allowing the sphincter to settle and providing access for a check cholangiogram before removal - **or a choledochoduodenostomy (choledocho-duodenostomy)** is constructed, draining the duct directly into the duodenum, the drainage option favored for a dilated duct with multiple or primary stones; and **B- transduodenal sphincterotomy and stone extraction**: the duodenum is opened over the ampulla, the sphincter is divided from below and the stone extracted - the approach for a stone impacted at the ampulla itself. Once the duct is cleared, the gallbladder (the factory of secondary stones) is scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy so the duct does not simply refill.
key_points: First-line: ERCP and sphincterotomy with stone extraction.
If failed: choledochotomy (CBD exploration).
Supraduodenal route: stone removal then T-tube or choledochoduodenostomy.
Transduodenal route: sphincterotomy and stone extraction (for impacted distal/ampullary stones).

check.prompt: ERCP and sphincterotomy have failed to clear a large impacted stone in the distal CBD in a fit patient. What is the next step?
options: Surgical CBD exploration by choledochotomy (supraduodenal or transduodenal)
Repeat ERCP every month until the stone dissolves
Long-term dissolution therapy with bile salts
Observation with a fat-free diet only
check.explanation_ar: عند فشل التنظير العلاجي تُفتح القناة الجامعة جراحيًا: فتح فوق الاثني عشري مع أنبوب T أو مفاغرة قناة واثني عشر، أو قطع العاصرة عبر الاثني عشري لاستخراج الحصى؛ فالذوبان الدوائي والانتظار لا مكان لهما مع انسداد معتمد.

تنظير القنوات الصفراوية والبنكرياس بالرجعي عبر الاثني عشر؛ تشخيصي وعلاجي معًا، ومع قطع العاصرة يستخرج حصى القناة الجامعة ويصرف الشجرة الصفراوية.

فتح القناة الجامعة للصفراء جراحيًا لاستكشافها واستخراج الحصى عند فشل التنظير العلاجي.

مفاغرة القناة الجامعة مع الاثني عشر؛ خيار تصريف وإصلاح بعد استخراج حصى القناة أو في متلازمة ميريزي.
يرقان انسدادي: ارتفاع البيليروبين المباشر والفوسفاتاز القلوي مع إنزيمات خلوية طبيعية تقريبًا، مع بول غامق وبراز فاتح.
